To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cone penetration in silitic material results in the formation of both dilative and contractive zones, the relative importance of these zones being dependent on the penetration speed.

(1) The cone penetration resistance is controlled by the local porosity, and the pore pressure is influenced by the local porosities and particle orientations in the zones around the penetrometer; (2) the local porosity and particle orientations in zones around the penetrometers are controlled by the local deformation mechanisms; and (3) the deformation mechanisms in zones around the probes are controlled by the penetration rate.

cone penetration in silterates results in the formation of contractive and dilating zones around the cone shaft and tip, and that the macro response of the soil during the test is controlled by the balance between these two processes.

the development of the microstructural changes around the cone during penetration and their influence on the macroscopic response of silt during cone penetration tests.
the microstructural aspects of cone penetration in silitic soil and the relationship of microstructural features to the macro response.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the microstructural analysis of thin sections is a powerful tool for studying the soil deformation mechanisms and the failure modes during CPTU, which can be used to improve our understanding of cone penetration testing in fine-grained soils.
the cone penetration resistance is not only controlled by the soil properties but also by the microstructure of the soil around the cone tip.
